note.explanation: Matter occurs in different states. The arrangement, spacing and movement of particles, and the strength of the forces between them, help explain how solids, liquids and gases differ.
examples: A gas has particles far apart and is easily compressed.
A solid has particles closely packed in fixed positions and has a definite shape.
note.checkAnswer: Plasma is a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons.
note.simple: Matter is the material around us. Its particles can be arranged and move in different ways, giving matter different states.
note.title: States of Matter
steps: Recall its particle arrangement and movement.
Connect those particle features to the state’s properties.
note.answer: Plasma is a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons.

options: Its particles are fixed in an orderly arrangement.
Its particles are very widely apart, with no order.
Its particles are close together and move randomly.
Its particles have very high kinetic energy and are ionized.

rationales: This describes the closely packed, orderly particles of a crystalline solid.
This is correct because gas molecules are very widely apart with no order.

This describes plasma, which contains highly energetic particles.

examTips: Short questions may ask for the definition or an example of a state, such as plasma in the Sun or a fluorescent tube.
Constructed-response questions may ask you to describe supercritical fluids or explain how plasma forms in a fluorescent tube.
For comparisons, earn marks by stating a feature for each state, such as particle spacing and movement.
Descriptive questions can ask for a full explanation; include the defining feature and the properties that follow from it.
Use the textbook’s key terms: widely apart, closely attached, fixed positions, partially ionized, highly compressed and exotic states.

steps.why: These features identify a solid in the textbook’s description.
steps.text: Solid particles are closely packed and have very strong attractions.

steps.why: Fixed positions distinguish solid particles from freely moving gas molecules.
steps.text: The particles remain fixed at their positions, where they can oscillate about their mean positions.

steps.why: The particle arrangement explains the solid’s macroscopic properties.
steps.text: Solids have a definite shape and fixed volume and are relatively incompressible and rigid.

example.question: Use particle arrangement and movement to describe a solid.
example.answer: Solid particles are closely packed, strongly attracted and fixed at their positions, where they can oscillate about their mean positions. Solids have a definite shape and fixed volume.

explain.title: Matter and its states
explain.body: Anything other than energy which carries weight and occupies volume is called matter. A state of matter is one of the many distinct forms in which matter can exist. The three primary states are solid, liquid and gas; plasma is also observed in everyday life.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: Gas molecules are very widely apart, have no order and experience very weak intermolecular forces. Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly, with significant intermolecular forces. Solid particles are closely packed, strongly attracted and fixed at their positions, where they can oscillate about their mean positions.

explain.title: Plasma and intermediate states
explain.body: Plasma is composed of particles with very high kinetic energy and can be considered a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons. Supercritical fluids are highly compressed states showing properties of gases and liquids. Liquid crystals have properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.

explain.title: Graphene and exotic states
explain.body: Graphene is a two-dimensional crystal consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern. States of matter not commonly encountered are called exotic states of matter.

mistakes: Do not say that gas molecules are close together; they are very widely apart.
Do not say that solid particles travel freely; they remain fixed at their positions and oscillate about their mean positions.
Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: the section describes plasma as a partially ionized gas.
Do not confuse a supercritical fluid with a liquid crystal: the former shows properties of gases and liquids, while the latter has properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
When comparing graphite and graphene, do not omit the key difference: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms.
